\chapter{Looking after loved ones}
\label{ch:ar-looking-after-loved-ones}
\hlchaptermodality{533}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that someone looked after, spoiled, held or stood by a loved one.}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 533: I can say that someone looked after, spoiled, held or stood by a loved one.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{اعتنى} (iʿtanā)}{اعتنى (iʿtanā)}]{\ar{اعتنى} (iʿtanā) — to look after}

\label{lesson:AR-C533-itana}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to lead a life, then the Arabic for to die.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{اعتنى}}
\textbf{\ar{اعتنى}} — \emph{iʿtanā} — \textquotedblleft{}to look after\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{تعتني} \ar{أختي} \ar{بجدتي} \ar{المريضة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{taʿtanī ukhtī bi-jaddatī al-marīḍa.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My sister looks after my sick grandmother.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يعتني}, \emph{yaʿtanī}.

It takes \ar{بـ} for the person.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{اعتنى}} (\emph{iʿtanā}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʿ-n-y}, \textquotedblleft{}to concern, to occupy\textquotedblright{} (Lane). ʿĀnā, to suffer, is from the same root; Form VIII iʿtanā is to make a person your concern.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iʿtanā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iʿtanā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{taʿtanī ukhtī bi-jaddatī al-marīḍa.} — My sister looks after my sick grandmother.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to lead a life, then the Arabic for to die, then say \emph{iʿtanā} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{اعتنى} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To look after\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{دلل} (dallala)}{دلل (dallala)}]{\ar{دلل} (dallala) — to pamper; to spoil (a child)}

\label{lesson:AR-C533-dallala}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to die, then the Arabic for to look after.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{دلل}}
\textbf{\ar{دلل}} — \emph{dallala} — \textquotedblleft{}to pamper; to spoil (a child)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{يدلل} \ar{الجد} \ar{حفيده} \ar{الصغير}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{yudallilu al-jadd ḥafīdahu aṣ-ṣaghīr.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The grandfather spoils his little grandson.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يدلل}, \emph{yudallil}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{دلل}} (\emph{dallala}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{d-l-l}, \textquotedblleft{}to direct; to be coquettish\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Form II dallala is to pamper. Dalla, to show the way, which you know, has the same letters.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dallala}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yudallilu al-jadd ḥafīdahu aṣ-ṣaghīr.} — The grandfather spoils his little grandson.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to die, then the Arabic for to look after, then say \emph{dallala} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{حضن} (ḥaḍana)}{حضن (ḥaḍana)}]{\ar{حضن} (ḥaḍana) — to cradle; to hold in one's arms}

\label{lesson:AR-C533-hadana}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to look after, then the Arabic for to pamper.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{حضن}}
\textbf{\ar{حضن}} — \emph{ḥaḍana} — \textquotedblleft{}to cradle; to hold in one's arms\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{حضنت} \ar{الأم} \ar{طفلها} \ar{الباكي}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ḥaḍanat al-umm ṭiflahā al-bākī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The mother held her crying child in her arms.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يحضن}, \emph{yaḥḍun}.

It also means to foster a child.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{حضن}} (\emph{ḥaḍana}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ḥ-ḍ-n}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold to the bosom; to rear\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives yaḥḍunu as its present.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to look after, then the Arabic for to pamper, then say \emph{ḥaḍana} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{ساند} (sānada)}{ساند (sānada)}]{\ar{ساند} (sānada) — to stand by}

\label{lesson:AR-C533-sanada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to pamper, then the Arabic for to cradle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{ساند}}
\textbf{\ar{ساند}} — \emph{sānada} — \textquotedblleft{}to stand by\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{ساندني} \ar{أخي} \ar{في} \ar{وقت} \ar{صعب}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{sānadanī akhī fī waqt ṣaʿb.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My brother stood by me at a difficult time.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يساند}, \emph{yusānid}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{ساند}} (\emph{sānada}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{s-n-d}, \textquotedblleft{}to lean on, to prop\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Form III sānada is to be a prop for someone.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{حبيب} (ḥabīb)}{حبيب (ḥabīb)}]{\ar{حبيب} (ḥabīb) — a loved one, a darling}

\label{lesson:AR-C533-habib}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to cradle, then the Arabic for to stand by.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{حبيب}}
\textbf{\ar{حبيب}} — \emph{ḥabīb} — \textquotedblleft{}a loved one, a darling\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{سافر} \ar{حبيبها} \ar{وانتظرته} \ar{سنة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{sāfara ḥabībuhā wa-intaẓarathu sana.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Her sweetheart went away and she waited a year for him.
\end{quote}

Plural: \ar{أحباب}, \emph{aḥbāb}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{حبيب}} (\emph{ḥabīb}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ḥ-b-b}, \textquotedblleft{}to love\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Ḥubb, love, and aḥabba, to love, which you know, share the root.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}
